register.title: User registration - process description
caption1_text: The registration process begins on a page with a form that allows the user to enter their email address and password.
I used the &Formik& library to manage the form, which simplifies managing the state of form fields, error handling, and the process of sending data to the backend.
Data validation occurs before the form is submitted—the &Yup& library checks the email address for validity and checks whether the fields are empty.
After the form is submitted, the login details are passed to the backend, where they are verified against the data stored in the &users.json& file.
register.caption2_text: Before the form submits data, &Yup& checks its validity—for example, the email address format and password matching—allowing for data validation before sending to the backend.
register.caption3_text1: After successful validation, I call the onHandleSubmit function. In this function, I prepare callbacks responsible for the frontend's response to success or error and pass the data to the &API&.
caption3_text2: I create the &onSuccess& function → it displays a message and redirects to the login.
I create the &onError& function → it displays an error message.
I execute the request via postRegister.
register.caption4: 4. Sending Data to the API (Fetch + JSON)
caption4_text1: After submitting the form, the user's data is sent to the backend using the &Fetch API&. The data is transmitted in &JSON& format, so it's converted using &JSON.stringify& before sending. The Content-Type: application/json header tells the backend &(Express)& how to read it.
The request is structured as an &HTTP POST&, and the body contains the data sent for registration. After receiving the server's response, the frontend executes the prepared callbacks:
caption4_text2: in case of success → &onSuccess()&, message + redirect
in case of error → &onError()&, error displayed to the user
caption5_text: On the server side, &Express& handles registration. Data in &JSON& format is sent to the /register endpoint.

The data is then compared against the existing database. The &readUsers()& function reads the user data from the database and assigns it to a variable. If the user isn't already in the database, we proceed to encrypt the password using &bcypt.hash&, so that passwords aren't stored in plain text.

In the next step, I create an ID for each user using &uuidv4()&. This unique identifier (&ID&), along with the hashed password and the initially received email address, are saved in the new newUser object.

The newUser object itself, containing the user data, also contains empty fields such as nickname, firstname, lastname, city, phone number, and description, which the user can complete and edit in their user panel.

The object also contains an avatar, assigned a random graphic generated by piscum. Ultimately, in the production version, it will be possible to upload your own graphic here using, for example, &S3 BUCKET&.
This object, containing user data, is added to the users array (&users.push()&) and saved in users.json (&writeUsers()&).
caption6_text1: Users are stored in the users.json file. In this project, I'm using a simple database based on the &users.json& file to store user data. Due to the nature of the project, there was no need to set up a professional database (DB).
The &readUsers()& function allows you to read user data and then:
caption6_text2: return an empty array if the database is empty (no users),
caption6_text3: The &writeUsers()& function overwrites the existing file with an array of new data.
I refer to both the readUsers() and writeUsers() functions in several endpoints.
register.caption7_text1: After receiving a positive response, the frontend:
caption7_text2: displays a success message and runs goToLogin()
after 2 seconds, redirects to the /login page.
register.caption7_text3: This ensures that after successful registration, the user is redirected to the login page.

login.title: User Login – Process Description
caption1_text: Similar to user registration, the login process begins on a page with a form that allows the user to enter their email address and password.
The entire form process is powered by the &Formik& library, which simplifies managing form field states, error handling, and the process of sending data to the backend.
Data validation is performed before the form is submitted using the &Yup& library, which checks for correct email formatting and password validity.
After clicking the Submit button, the form passes the data to the &onHandleSubmit& function, which initiates the login process and transfers the data via the &API& to the backend.
caption2_text: Before the form submits data to the API, Yup validates it. In this case, it checks the correct format of the entered email address and whether the password field is empty.
This allows the user to receive error notifications more quickly, without having to submit the form to the backend.
caption3_text1: After successful validation, the &onHandleSubmit& function is executed, containing further data flow instructions and the appropriate frontend action.
caption3_text2: I create an onSuccess function – triggered when the backend returns a valid token,
I create an onError function – displaying a message about incorrect data,
I call the postLogin function, which sends the login data to the backend.
login.caption3_text3: This is where communication with the &API& begins.
login.caption4: 4. Sending Data to the API (Fetch + JSON)
caption4_text1: Similar to the registration process, after submitting the login form, user data is sent to the backend using the &Fetch API&. The data is transmitted in JSON format, so it is converted using &JSON.stringify& before sending. There is also a Content-Type:application/json header that tells the backend (&Express&) how it should be read. The request is structured as an &HTTP POST&, with the login data passed in the body.
After receiving the server's response, the frontend executes the prepared callbacks:
caption4_text2: If the backend returns a 200 status, the &onSuccess()& callback is triggered.
If the data is invalid (401 status), an &onError()& callback is displayed.
login.caption4_text3: &This is where the similarities between the registration and login processes end. Entering data into the form, validating it, and sending it to the API are similar in both cases. The data is then sent to the server, where the path is slightly different.&
caption5_text: Data is sent to the endpoint via &POST /login&. Similar to registration, the &readUsers()& function is executed, which reads the contents of the &users.json& file.

Next, the email address provided during login (which was sent to the endpoint) is compared with the contents of the existing database. If the address is found in the database, the password is checked for validity.
The encrypted password assigned to the previously filtered email address in the database is compared with the password sent to the endpoint from the login form (&bcrypt.comapre&).

If the passwords match, a &JWT token& (JSON WEB TOKEN) is generated, containing the user ID and the token's validity (1h). The token is then sent back to the frontend, where it is stored in the local state (&useContext&) and in &sessionStorage&.
caption6_text: After logging in and receiving the token, the frontend executes the next instruction contained in &onHandleSubmit& – a query to the &/readUserData& endpoint. This endpoint is responsible for retrieving the user's full data from the database so that the frontend can save it in the application context (&useContext&).

This time, the query is sent using the &GET& method (&fetch API&). In addition to the previously used header: &Content-Type: application/json&, an authorization header: &Authorization: Bearer token& is also passed to the backend.

When the data reaches the &/readUserData& endpoint, the &verifyUser middleware& is first launched to verify the user's token. The detailed operation of this middleware is described in the next section.
If the user has been successfully authenticated, the backend reads the JSON file with the user data using the &readUsers()& function.

In the next step, the user &ID& from the received &token& is compared with the user IDs stored in the database. If the IDs match, the remaining information assigned to the user is retrieved. All user data is then returned: email, nickname, first name, last name, avatar, city, phone number, description, etc.
If the user doesn't exist or the token is invalid, the backend returns an appropriate error message.
After receiving the data from the server, the frontend stores it in the context (&useContext()&).
&This allows the frontend to immediately display user data after login without waiting for an additional page reload (e.g., a nickname in the page header if the user entered it).&
caption7_text: &VeryfyUser&, a &middleware& that runs before executing the actual code in the endpoint, checks whether the request sent to the server contains a header with a token (&Bearer Token&).

If the token is present, &jwt.verify& decodes it using the &.env& environment variable along with the secret key. Then, the resulting user &ID&, previously contained in the token, is passed as a variable to the &/readUserData& endpoint.
login.caption8: 8. Saving User Data in the useContext
caption8_text1: The frontend saves selected data in the global UserContext (&useContext()&), using the passed setters (&useState()&).
caption8_text3: The context is defined in the main application file (&App.tsx&), which contains a &router& with paths to individual application pages. The &provider& that provides data from the context forwards it to all paths in the project, allowing all application pages to access and edit the data.

The &handleSetToken()& function is crucial here. After receiving the &token&, it saves it in the browser's memory. This prevents the token stored in &sessionStorage& (and not just in the context) from being reset when components are re-rendered.

The next step is &useEffect()&, which retrieves the current &token& from the browser's &sessionStorage& upon re-rendering the components, then recreates the individual data states (completes the context). To do this, a fetch to the &/readUserData& endpoint is performed again.

&This ensures that after refreshing the page or navigating to another page of the application, the user remains logged in, and the context containing user data (e.g., the nickname in the page header) remains up-to-date.&
login.caption9_text: After successfully logging in and displaying the message You are logged in!, we proceed to the last statement in &onHandleSubmit: goToHome()&. After 2 seconds, the user is automatically redirected to the home page.

userPanel.title: User Panel - Process Description
userPanel.caption1: 1. Redirection after logging in + fetching user data
caption1_text: After logging in, the user is redirected to the application's main page. First, the instructions in &useEffect()& are executed to retrieve the current user data from the backend. The process of connecting to the server and fetching data is described in the next section.

If the user has been logged in and their data has been successfully retrieved, a section with user data such as their &ID& and &email& address is displayed. At the end of the section, a button redirecting to the user panel displays, where all data can be accessed and edited.
The user panel URL uses the ID previously retrieved in fetch.
caption2_text: Using the &token& we retrieve from the global context (&usecontext()&), we perform a &fetch& by connecting to the &/me& endpoint. To do this, we send a request using the &GET method&, using headers including the '&Bearer token&' authorization.
We read the received data in the form of a Response object in &JSON& format, returning the &ID& and &email&.
caption3_text: Endpoint &/me& works similarly to &/getData& described in the login process. First, the &veryfiUser middleware& (also described in point 7 of the login process) is launched, which, based on the received &token&, decodes it and returns the decrypted user &ID& previously contained in the token.

After successful authentication, we return to endpoint &/me&, which runs the &readUsers()& function, which in turn reads the user data file. The ID obtained after decrypting the token is compared with the user IDs from the database. Once a matching ID is found, the remaining data for that user is retrieved and sent to the frontend with a status of 200.
userPanel.caption4: 4. Going to the user panel: downloading full data
caption4_text1: After clicking the Go to user settings button, the user is redirected to the page: &userpage:userId&.
Another &useEffect& is executed in the user panel, which:
caption4_text2: sends the token to the backend again (endpoint &/readUserData&),
the backend returns the full data stored in the database: email, nickname, first name, last name, avatar, city, phone number, description, etc.
the data is set in the component state (userData) and simultaneously in the global context (&UserContext&).
caption4_text3: This ensures that the form always displays the current data of the logged-in user. &A detailed description of the /readUserData endpoint can be found in point 6 of the login process description.&
The user panel operates in two modes:
caption4_text4: data retrieved from the backend is displayed,
data is presented in an aesthetically pleasing user card,
the Edit Data button is visible.
caption4_text5: Clicking Edit Data activates form mode:
caption4_text6: Formika form filled with current data (initialValues=userData),
field validation using Yup (email, nickname, first name, last name, phone number, etc.); the user can edit any of their data.
userPanel.caption5: 5. Saving data – sending changes to the backend.
caption5_text: After editing the data, the user submits the form (validation, similar to the registration and login forms, is performed using the &Yup& library), which triggers the &handleSubmit()& function. Its task is to collect all currently filled-out fields and call the &updateUserData()& function, which is responsible for sending the changes to the backend.

The update process is multi-stage. First, the application checks whether a valid user token is still present in the global context. If so, the data entered in the form is saved in JSON format (&API&) and sent to endpoint &/updateUser& using the &PUT method&. The user token, passed as &Authorization: Bearer Token&, is used in the headers, allowing the backend to clearly confirm which user sent the request.

If the backend saves the data correctly, the component updates the local state (&setDataUpdate(true)&) and disables edit mode, returning to the preview view. In case of errors, an appropriate message is displayed, and the backend itself returns the error status visible in the console.
userPanel.caption6: 6. Handling the update endpoint on the backend side
caption6_text: The endpoint responsible for updating user data is based on the &PUT method& and the previously created &verifyUser middleware& (described in detail in point 7 of the login process). This middleware receives the token sent in the header and decrypts the user ID to be updated from it.

After successful authorization, the endpoint retrieves all fields from the request body that can be changed, such as: email address, nickname, first name, last name, phone number, avatar, and user description. The backend then finds the user with the provided &ID& in the database (in this case, in the &JSON& file with user data).

If the user exists, the backend performs the update. The key feature here is the mechanism of partial data overwriting — each field is assigned either The new value sent by the frontend, or the old value if the user hasn't made any changes.

After the process is complete, the backend saves the updated user list (&writeUsers()&) and returns a response with a message confirming the successful update. If the user cannot be found or an error occurs, the endpoint returns a 404 or 500 status, along with a description of the error.
userPanel.text_bottom: Register or log in and test how the user panel works

frontend.title: Frontend - technology description
frontend.caption1: 1. The role of React in the project
caption1_text: The application's &frontend& was built as a &single-page application& based on &React& and &React Router&. The project's structure is based on a clear division into page views (&pages&), reusable components (&components&), and an &API& communication layer.

The application uses React contexts to manage the global state of the logged-in user. Session data (token, user data) is stored in the &UserContext&, allowing access to it anywhere in the application without the need to pass props. The session state is initialized based on data stored in &sessionStorage&, ensuring the user remains logged in after a page refresh.
The component logic is based on functional hooks (&useState, useEffect, useContext&), and repetitive mechanisms have been separated into their &own Hooks& (e.g., screen width support).

&Forms& (registration, login, and editing user data) were implemented using the &Formik& and &Yup& libraries, ensuring consistent management of form state, data validation, and client-side error handling.

UI components are separated from the backend communication logic — &HTTP requests& have been separated into a separate &API& layer. This ensures the frontend remains readable, easy to test, and &ready for further expansion&.
caption2_text: The project structure is based on a clear division of responsibilities between individual components. Page views are located in the &pages& directory and are responsible for the logic of specific application screens. Common components, such as &layouts&, &headers&, and &footers&, have been separated into separate directories.
&Layout& components are responsible for the common structure of application pages, ensuring a consistent appearance and separating the presentation layer from the logic of individual views.
frontend.caption3_text: &React Router v6& with a &createBrowserRouter& -based configuration was used to handle routing. Both &static& and &dynamic routes& were defined, e.g., a user page containing an identifier parameter.
caption4_text: The logged-in user's state is managed globally using the &React context& mechanism. The context stores key information, such as &user data& and the &authorization token&. This allows all application components to access the current user state without the need to pass props through multiple levels.

Additionally, the &token& is stored in &sessionStorage& , which allows the user session to be recreated after a page refresh. When the application is re-rendered, There's an initialization mechanism that retrieves current user data from the &backend& based on the saved token.
caption5_text: The project uses the &Formik library& to handle forms. It allows for convenient management of form field states, data submission, and error response. Each form (&login, registration, editing user data&) is based on the same, consistent mechanism.

Data validation is implemented using the &Yup library&, which allows for client-side data validation. This ensures that the user receives immediate error notification, and the backend is not burdened with invalid queries.
frontend.caption6_text: The project uses &custom React hooks& that allow you to separate repetitive logic from components. An example is a hook that handles screen width, which responds to &browser window size changes& and ensures proper event listener removal.
frontend.caption7: 7. Styling Components – CSS Modules and Sass
caption7_text: The frontend was styled using &CSS Modules& combined with &Sass/SCSS&. This allows each component to be assigned a set of classes that are isolated from the rest of the application, preventing conflicts when binding the page.
To maintain color and typography consistency, I use global variable files such as &_colors.scss& and &_typography.scss&.

For &responsiveness&, I used &mixins& (max-width and min-width) defined in &_breakpoints.scss&. This allows the page and component layout to adapt to different resolutions depending on the screen width.
The &nesting& and &modifiers& used in .scss files allow you to easily assign different variants to components depending on the context.

api.title: API - frontend-backend communication
api.caption1_text: The API layer acts as an intermediary between the frontend and the backend. The frontend does not have direct access to data, and all operations are performed through explicitly defined &REST API endpoints&.
api.caption2_text: Each function in the API layer corresponds to a single backend endpoint and handles a specific operation, such as logging in, registering, or retrieving user data.
caption3_text: The project uses &TypeScript&, which ensures data consistency between the frontend and the backend. Data types describe the structure of API responses and help avoid errors resulting from incompatible data.
This allows the frontend to know, even at the coding stage, what data it will receive from the &API& and how to properly process it.
caption4_text: Endpoints requiring authorization use the &Bearer Token& mechanism. The &JWT token& is sent in the &Authorization& header, which allows the backend to uniquely identify the user making the request.
The &token& is retrieved from the &global application state&, and its presence determines access to protected resources.
api.caption5_text: After the user logs in, the &backend& returns a &JWT token&, which is stored in the &application context& and in &sessionStorage&. The token is then used for subsequent &API& requests.

server.title: Server - technology description
server.caption1: 1. The server's role in the project
server.caption1_text: The server acts as an &API& provider and is responsible for authorization and operations on user data. It does not render views or manage the UI layer—the entire interface is implemented in React.
caption2_text: The backend was built based on the Node.js environment and the &Express& framework. Express is responsible for handling &routing&, &middleware&, and the structure of &REST API endpoints&.

The project uses &CORS& middleware, which enables secure communication between the frontend and backend running on &different addresses&. This allows the client application to execute API requests without issues related to browser security policies.
&The detailed operation of the verifyUser middleware is described in Use Case section in point 7 of the login process.&
server.caption_2_button: Go to the login process description
caption3_text: The authentication process is based on &JWT&. User passwords are encrypted using the &bcrypt library&, which protects data from being stored in the clear.
The &middleware& responsible for token verification protects endpoints requiring authorization and ensures that only the logged-in user has access to their data.
caption4_text: User data is stored in a &JSON& file, which acts as a simplified database. This solution was deliberately implemented to focus on the application architecture and data flow, rather than on the configuration of an external database.
The data reading and writing mechanisms have been separated into separate functions, facilitating a potential migration to a full-fledged database in the future.
&Reading and writing user data is described in detail in point 6 of the registration process.&
server.caption_4_button: Go to the registration process description

hero.header: This page presents a web application project created to showcase my skills and approach to building applications based on the React library.
hero.text1: From the user's perspective, the application offers three main functionalities:
list: user panel with data editing capabilities
hero.text2: Each section of the project presents a different aspect of working on the application—from the user interface and data validation, through API communication, to server logic, and shows the processes behind its development.

box1.title: Registration
box1.text: The registration form provides real-time data validation and guides the user step-by-step, informing them about data accuracy and potential errors before submitting the form. It integrates directly with the backend API, ensuring data consistency and error tolerance.
box1.button2: Go to the registration process description

box2.title: Login
box2.text: The login module handles the entire user authorization process, including data validation, error handling, and communication with the server. After sending the data to the server, the system decrypts the password and compares it with the existing database. After successful login, a token is generated that allows access to the secure resources of the application. After 1 hour, the token expires and the user is logged out.
box2.button2: Go to the login process description

box3.title: User Panel
box3.text: The user panel allows you to manage your account data, view information, and interact with the system after logging in. The view responds dynamically to the status of the application and data retrieved from the API. The whole thing has been designed as a central place for user management in the application.
box3.button1: Go to user panel process description

box1.title: Frontend
box1.text: The application frontend was built based on React's component-based architecture, which ensures code readability and easy expansion. The user interface is responsive and visually consistent (CSS Modules), and the application logic has been separated from the presentation layer.

box2.title: Api
box2.text: The API layer is responsible for communication between the frontend and the server. It provides authorization support, data validation, and logical grouping of endpoints. The API has been designed in accordance with REST principles, which facilitates its development and integration with other systems.

box3.title: Server
box3.text: The server handles logic, authorization, and communication with the database (JSON). During user registration, data is encrypted before it reaches the database, while during login, middleware is launched to decrypt the data, ensuring security and code structure readability.
